blocks.text: The previous topic, Types of Version Control, introduced local, centralized, and distributed systems side by side at a survey level. This topic goes one level deeper into just the centralized-versus-distributed comparison specifically, since that is the choice that actually matters for essentially every real engineering decision today: local VCS is not a live option, but teams genuinely do still choose between (or inherit) centralized and distributed tooling.

Two ideas anchor this deeper comparison: the very real single-point-of-failure risk that comes from a centralized architecture, and the somewhat counterintuitive fact that distributed systems like Git, despite having no architecturally required center, still end up organized around a conventional "central" remote in almost every real team.
1. The Single Point of Failure, In Depth

In a centralized VCS (CVCS), one server is the sole holder of the authoritative, complete history. Every commit goes through it, and in most CVCS designs, developer working copies hold only the current checked-out files, not the full history behind them. This means the server is not just a convenience, it is a structural dependency for nearly every meaningful operation.

blocks.alt: What breaks when the central server in a CVCS fails
blocks.caption: A CVCS server outage does not just block new commits, it can block history access and downstream automation as well.

blocks.text: The practical blast radius of this is larger than "commits are paused." Continuous integration pipelines that pull from the central server stall. Code review tooling built on top of it becomes unreachable. Auditors or incident responders who need to inspect history are blocked until the server is restored. This is why CVCS deployments typically require serious, dedicated investment in server redundancy and backups, the risk has to be engineered away rather than being absent by design.

blocks.title: This is a real operational cost, not just theory
blocks.content: Teams running centralized systems at scale (large SVN or Perforce deployments) typically run the server on redundant, monitored infrastructure specifically because of this risk, essentially paying an ongoing engineering cost to compensate for an architectural weak point. Distributed systems get equivalent resilience largely for free, as a side effect of every clone already holding full history.

blocks.text: A distributed VCS clone contains the entire history, which means the vast majority of everyday Git operations never need to talk to a server at all. Committing, branching, merging, viewing history, diffing, and stashing are all purely local operations against data you already have.

blocks.alt: What still works with no network connection
blocks.caption: The core Git workflow, commit, branch, log, merge, stash, works completely offline; only push/pull require a network.

blocks.text: Only synchronization operations, git push and git fetch/git pull, actually require reaching a remote. This is a fundamentally different experience from a CVCS, where the equivalent of "commit" is itself a network operation to the central server, and being offline meaningfully limits what you can do.

code.content:
# A full day of real work, entirely offline
git switch -c feature/offline-mode
# ... edit files across several commits ...
git add -p                      # stage changes interactively
git commit -m "Add offline cache layer"
git log --oneline --graph        # inspect the history you've built, no network needed
git diff main                     # compare your branch against main, no network needed

# Only this step needs connectivity, whenever it's available:
git push origin feature/offline-mode

blocks.title: Real scenario
blocks.content: A developer works through a multi-hour flight, making a dozen small commits, creating two exploratory branches, and reviewing the last month of project history to understand some old code, all without connectivity. On landing, a single git push synchronizes everything. The equivalent day on a CVCS would have been largely blocked from the moment the plane took off.

blocks.text: 3. Every Clone Is a Full, Equal Peer

Because every clone in a distributed system carries the complete history, there is no architectural distinction between a developer's local repository and whatever remote everyone happens to push to. A remote is, technically, just another Git repository somewhere else that your local repository knows how to talk to.

blocks.alt: Every clone is architecturally equal to the origin remote
blocks.caption: A DVCS clone and the remote it syncs with are the same kind of thing: a full repository with complete history.

blocks.text: This is easy to say and genuinely surprising the first time you see it in practice: two developers can push and pull directly between their own machines, with no shared server involved at all, as long as one can reach the other over the network.

blocks.alt: Two developers syncing directly with no central server
blocks.caption: Git supports direct peer-to-peer syncing between developer machines; a hosted remote like GitHub is convention, not requirement.

code.content:
# Genuinely peer-to-peer Git, no GitHub involved
git remote add alice ssh://alice@192.168.1.42/home/alice/project.git
git fetch alice
git merge alice/main

# alice, meanwhile, can pull directly from you the same way
# ssh://you@192.168.1.17/home/you/project.git

blocks.text: 4. Why Teams Still Use a Central Remote by Convention

If every clone is a full peer, why does nearly every real team still organize around one shared remote like GitHub or GitLab? Because peer equality is an architectural property of the storage model, it says nothing about the coordination and tooling value a hosted, agreed-upon hub adds on top: pull requests, code review, permissions, issue tracking, and CI/CD integration.

blocks.alt: A conventional central hub adds value beyond raw storage
blocks.caption: GitHub is not required by Git architecture, but the coordination features built on top of it are why teams standardize on one.

blocks.text: So the honest framing is: Git itself does not require a center, but real engineering organizations benefit enormously from agreeing on one anyway, for the same reason a company benefits from everyone agreeing to use the same shared calendar even though nothing forces them to. The word "origin" for the default remote name is itself just a convention, not a special designation Git enforces.

items: Architecturally: every clone, including the one on GitHub, is an equal peer with full history.
Operationally: teams designate one remote as the shared source of truth for coordination, reviews, and automation.
The distinction matters because it explains why Git still gives you full offline capability and disaster recovery even though, day to day, it feels centralized around GitHub.

blocks.title: Common pitfall
blocks.content: New Git users sometimes assume GitHub being down means Git itself is broken. It does not: local commits, branches, and history all keep working, only pushing and pulling to that specific remote are affected. Distinguishing "GitHub is down" from "Git is down" is a direct, practical consequence of the peer-equality property covered in this section.

blocks.text: Building on the single-point-of-failure discussion earlier, it is worth comparing recovery specifically. In a CVCS, if the central server's data is lost with no separate backup, recovery is limited to whatever any individual working copy happens to have checked out, which is typically far less than the full history.

blocks.alt: Recovering from a lost server in each model
blocks.caption: Losing the sole centralized server can mean real data loss; losing one distributed remote does not, since any clone has the full history.

blocks.text: In a distributed system, losing the shared remote (even a hosted one like GitHub, however unlikely) is a non-event for the history itself: any developer's local clone already has everything. Recovery is just pushing that clone's history to a freshly created remote and updating everyone's origin to point at it.

code.content:
# Recovering after losing the shared remote entirely
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/team/project-new.git
git push origin --all       # push every branch
git push origin --tags       # push every tag
# the "new" remote now has the exact same full history as before

blocks.title: A deliberate backup habit: git bundle
blocks.content: Beyond relying on developer clones informally, Git has a purpose-built tool for portable, offline backups: git bundle. It packages the entire repository (or specific branches) into one file that can be stored anywhere and later cloned from directly, no server required at all.

blocks.alt: Using git bundle as a portable, server-free backup
blocks.caption: git bundle packages full history into one portable file that can restore a repository without any server.

code.content:
git bundle create backup.bundle --all   # snapshot every branch and tag into one file
# later, on any machine:
git clone backup.bundle restored-project    # a fully working clone, no network involved

blocks.text: None of this makes centralized systems strictly worse in every dimension. A CVCS can be simpler to reason about for teams that genuinely never need offline work, and enforces a single authoritative history without any convention needed, since the architecture itself only allows one. Distributed systems trade that simplicity for resilience, offline capability, and merge-based parallelism, at the cost of needing an explicit convention (a designated remote) to get the coordination benefits a CVCS gives you automatically.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
points: Centralized VCS ties nearly every operation, and full disaster recovery, to one server; that server is a genuine single point of failure that has to be engineered around.
Distributed VCS gives every clone the complete history, enabling full offline commit/branch/log/merge and making disaster recovery close to automatic as long as work has been pushed anywhere.
Every clone in a distributed system, including a hosted remote like GitHub, is architecturally an equal peer; direct peer-to-peer syncing between developer machines is genuinely possible.

Teams still standardize on one "central" remote by convention, not architectural necessity, because of the coordination tooling (PRs, reviews, CI/CD, permissions) built on top of it, not because Git itself requires a center.
